analysis.one_liner: Gives federal regulators power to block, detain, and destroy imported food linked to repeated disease outbreaks and to ban repeat-offender importers.
analysis.headline: Introduced by Sen. Collins with 5 Republican cosponsors in May 1999, the bill never received a hearing or vote in the Senate Agriculture Committee and died when the Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let the Health and Human Services Secretary bar food from a specific producer, region, or country that keeps causing food poisoning outbreaks, and in emergencies block food after a single deadly outbreak. It would let regulators require imported food to sit in secure storage until cleared, order destruction of dangerous food at the importer's expense, stop 'port shopping' (re-offering refused food at a different port), and permanently ban importers who repeatedly bring in contaminated food. It would also double the customs bond for importers with violations, authorize more FDA inspectors and lab staff, and fund CDC grants to state and local health departments for tracking foodborne illness.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who eats food imported into the United States — roughly a large share of produce, seafood, and processed foods — would gain protection against contaminated imports. State and local health departments would get CDC grants to better detect and track foodborne outbreaks, and the FDA would gain authorized positions for more laboratory, inspection, and compliance staff.

how_it_helps.text: The bill lets HHS deny entry to food from a specific producer, growing area, or country that has been repeatedly linked to outbreaks or repeated adulteration findings, with an emergency path to block food after a single outbreak causing serious illness or death [S2][S3].

It treats several escape hatches as adulteration: distributing food before release, failing secure storage, failing a destruction order, re-offering refused food at another port without proving compliance, and importing under a debarred name [S2][S3].

Repeat and felony food-import violators can be debarred from importing food for at least a year, and importers with covered violations face bonds at twice the usual rate or more on a sliding scale [S2][S3].

It authorizes funding for additional FDA laboratory, inspection, and compliance personnel and CDC grants to state and local health departments for surveillance and prevention of foodborne disease, plus pathogen-detection research and public education [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Importers of food — and the foreign growers, manufacturers, and shippers whose products they bring in — would bear the cost: secure storage and destruction of suspect shipments at their own expense, doubled customs bonds after violations, debarment for repeat offenders, and lost sales when their products are denied entry. Some of those costs could show up in prices on imported foods, and foods from entire countries could be barred when problems are widespread.
analysis.who_pays_short: Food importers and foreign food producers

drawbacks.text: Food importers and foreign producers would face real costs — storage and destruction at their own expense, doubled bonds after violations, and denial of entry — which could raise prices on imported produce, seafood, and other foods [S2][S3].

The denial-of-entry system could cut off food from an entire growing area or country, affecting producers who had done nothing wrong; the bill mitigates this by requiring the agency to consider comments from affected parties and to lift denials if remedial evidence is submitted within 90 days [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real, documented hazard — contaminated food reaching American consumers through imports — with enforcement tools aimed at repeat offenders rather than honest importers, and includes comment periods and a 90-day automatic relief process as safeguards against overreach. The main costs fall on importers who repeatedly ship adulterated food, though honest importers would face some added delay and expense when inspections hold their goods.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or reported it out, so it never reached the Senate floor before the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Susan Collins introduced the Imported Food Safety Improvement Act on May 25, 1999, joined by five Republican cosponsors: Frist, Abraham, Snowe, Jeffords, and Coverdell [S1][S3][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry the same day [S5][S1].
The action history shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee report, no floor vote — before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Food importers and foreign food producers are better off: none of the bill's detention powers, debarment rules, doubled bonds, or port-shopping ban ever took effect, and the FDA got no additional inspectors. Consumers keep the pre-bill status quo in import oversight.

for.name: Susan Collins
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor [S1][S5].

for.name: Bill Frist, Spencer Abraham, Olympia Snowe, Jim Jeffords, and Paul Coverdell
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's five cosponsors [S3][S4].

against.name: Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and took no action on it — no hearing or markup — for the rest of the Congress [S1][S5].

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no voting record exists; sponsorship was all Republican (Collins plus 5 GOP cosponsors), but the record shows no stated opposition either.

industries.industry: Food importers (produce, seafood, and processed food)
industries.note: The bill would impose secure storage, destruction, and marking of suspect shipments at the importer's expense, doubled customs bonds after violations, and debarment of repeat offenders. These costs fall on an industry whose savings from weak oversight come at the public's expense in foodborne illness.

industries.industry: Foreign food producers, manufacturers, and exporters
industries.note: The bill would let HHS deny entry to food from a specific producer, growing area, or country with a record of repeated adulteration or outbreaks, and would require destruction of dangerous shipments. Producers from excluded regions would lose access to the U.S. market until they submitted remedial evidence.

industries.industry: U.S. produce and seafood retailers and restaurants
industries.note: Their supply would face more detentions and possible price increases on imported goods, but they would also benefit from fewer contaminated products reaching their customers and triggering recalls and liability.
The bill authorizes regulations allowing entities other than the FDA to collect and analyze import food samples, creating a role for outside labs under FDA integrity standards.
